text.p: Northeast Utilities said Monday it expects to report a signifcant fourth quarter loss.

The company said a late year surge in oil prices, a damaging December snowstorm and increased reserves to cover future nuclear operation and maintenance costs "are expected to significantly reduce Northeast Utilities fourth quarter finacial results."
NU is scheduled to report 1996 fourth quarter and full year results January 28, it noted. In the final quarter of 1995, the utility earned $64.2 million, or $0.50 per share.

Chief Financial Officer John Forsgren said NU expects to increase significantly the amount it is reserving to cover a portion of the higher expected opperation and maintenance costs at Millstone Station in 1997.
NU noted it reserved $40 million as of September 30, 1996.
"Now that we have a better idea of the work we'll be doing in 1997" the company is taking the charge, spokesman Jeffrey Kotkin said.
He declined to say how big the charge is expected to be, saying the amount will be disclosed along with fourth quarter results late this month.
Kotkin did say the December snowstorm cost about $10 million, or $0.05 per share.
NU also said the cost of replacing the power that Millstone would have generated rose to an estimated $110 million in the current quarter from about $80 million in the second quarter.
Forsgren said this increase was due in large part to "the rapdi increase in the price of oil in the fourth quarter.
Residual oil delivered to the utility's Middletown Station in Middletown, Conn., rose by about 25 percent to about $24 per barrel early this winter from $19 in late spring.
The price for the low sulphur product the plant is required to use had dropped below $20 a barrel in mid-Janyary, he said.
The utility said it expects to convert two of Middletown's four units to burn natural gas as well as oil, but the conversion is not expected to be complete until July.
Forsgren said NU now projects that higher nuclerar releated operation and maintenance costs, and higher replacement power costs, will continue well into 1997.

This is not a change in company expectations to have at least one Millstone unit back in operation by mid-year, Kotkin said. Rather, the statement is a reminder that the back to service dates projected a month ago still will involve significant costs for the company.
